by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes ARIZONA and an asset is tested under the homestead, personal-item, household-goods, firearm, or motor-vehicle provisions.
by_task.procedure: Treat a statutory dollar limit as an amount ceiling, not an eligibility threshold. Test each asset-exemption pair independently, so each described motor vehicle may cite § 33-1125(8) and a firearm may cite § 33-1125(10) even when its value exceeds the ceiling. Section 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings; § 33-1125(1) covers wearing apparel, not an ordinary pendant, necklace, or bracelet. For a residence, cite § 33-1101(A) as the asset exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not cite § 33-1101(B) or § 33-1121 as separate asset exemptions, and do not classify ordinary non-ring jewelry as wearing apparel or as an engagement or wedding ring without that fact.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes ARIZONA and a named asset requires both eligibility and protected-amount decisions.
by_task.procedure: Classify from the stated asset facts before calculating: clothing, including work-styled clothing absent an explicit contrary use, uses § 33-1125(1); only an engagement or wedding ring uses § 33-1125(4), so a pendant, bracelet, or anniversary ring does not. Household goods and appliances use § 33-1123, motor vehicles use § 33-1125(8), firearms use § 33-1125(10), prescribed prostheses use § 33-1125(9), domestic animals or household pets use § 33-1125(11), and a qualifying residence uses § 33-1101(A). Report the lesser of the whole asset value and the applicable ceiling: $15,000 for § 33-1123 or § 33-1125(8), $2,000 for § 33-1125(10) or § 33-1125(4), $500 for § 33-1125(1), and $400,000 for § 33-1101(A); the listed prosthesis and pet provisions use the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not eliminate an eligible asset because its value exceeds a ceiling, double these asset-level outputs merely because two debtors exist, infer nonpersonal use from work-style clothing, or assign a ring exemption without the required engagement-or-wedding fact.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes FEDERAL and an estate asset is being tested under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d).
by_task.procedure: Test § 522(d)(5) independently for every property type, even when a specific exemption also applies or the asset exceeds that specific exemption's ceiling. Retain both the specific citation and § 522(d)(5). Use § 522(d)(3) only for its listed household, apparel, appliance, book, animal, crop, or musical-instrument categories; use § 522(d)(4), not § 522(d)(3), for jewelry.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use federal § 522(d) exemptions when the supplied allowable jurisdiction excludes them, and do not emit § 522(b), § 522(d), or § 522(m) as asset-level alternatives.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes FEDERAL and a debtor-owned asset requires eligibility and amount decisions under § 522(d).
by_task.procedure: First add § 522(d)(5) as an independently eligible alternative for every property type. Its amount is the lesser of the whole asset value and $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1) capacity per debtor; with two debtors and fully available capacity, the asset-level maximum is $30,850. Then retain and value each independently applicable specific alternative: § 522(d)(1) up to $27,900 for a residence, § 522(d)(2) up to $4,450 for one motor vehicle, § 522(d)(3) up to $700 per particular listed item, § 522(d)(4) up to $1,875 for jewelry, § 522(d)(6) up to $2,800 for tools of trade, and § 522(d)(9) at the asset value for a professionally prescribed health aid.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not require the wildcard asset itself to be a residence, suppress § 522(d)(5) because a specific exemption applies or the asset exceeds a ceiling, classify jewelry or firearms under § 522(d)(3), copy a ceiling when the asset is worth less, or double a ceiling without a joint case and a statute that applies separately.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes ILLINOIS and the debtor owns personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Test 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent alternative for any other personal property. Retain it alongside applicable specific provisions such as necessary apparel, a motor vehicle, or a professionally prescribed health aid.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real property or business-use property, and do not discard a specific exemption when the general alternative also applies.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes ILLINOIS and an eligible personal asset requires an amount.
by_task.procedure:
For § 12-1001(b), report the lesser of the whole asset value and $4,000 for one debtor; for a jointly owned asset of two debtor spouses, combine the two observed per-debtor ceilings up to $8,000. Independently, § 12-1001(c) protects at most $2,400 of a motor vehicle, while necessary apparel under § 12-1001(a) and prescribed health aids under § 12-1001(e) use the asset's value. Emit every eligible alternative separately.
Execution example: Hypothetically, a jointly owned high-value vehicle of two debtor spouses has separate asset-level alternatives of $8,000 under § 12-1001(b) and $2,400 under § 12-1001(c); do not double the motor-vehicle ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 general-property ceiling for the $2,400 motor-vehicle ceiling or for an uncapped specific exemption, and do not leave a half-interest as the whole-asset result.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes OREGON and the named asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) independently for personal property, while retaining any applicable category-specific Oregon and federal citations.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property, and do not omit it merely because a more specific personal-property exemption also applies.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes OREGON and a debtor-owned personal-property asset requires eligibility and amount decisions.
by_task.procedure: First add § 18.345(1)(p) independently and report the lesser of the whole asset value and $400. Then retain and value each supported specific alternative under its own rule, including § 18.345(1)(b) for wearing apparel or jewelry, § 18.345(1)(f) for household goods or appliances, § 18.345(1)(d) for a vehicle, § 18.345(1)(h) for a prescribed health aid, and § 18.362 for a qualifying firearm.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to a homestead or other real property, omit it because another personal-property exemption applies, treat $400 as an eligibility threshold, double its asset-level output merely because two debtors are listed, or replace the correct apparel category with the household-goods category.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes PENNSYLVANIA and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption for any property. Retain it alongside every independently applicable federal or Pennsylvania-specific exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not replace a specific exemption with § 8123, and do not cite Pennsylvania provisions for property not owned by the debtor.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes PENNSYLVANIA and the named asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Make an independent Pennsylvania pass over every debtor-owned asset, including real property and business property, and add § 8123 whether or not another exemption applies. Report the lesser of the whole asset value and $300 for one debtor. For a jointly owned asset of two debtor spouses, § 8123 permits a combined asset-level amount up to $600, capped by value. Keep every independently eligible federal or Pennsylvania-specific alternative and calculate it under its own rule.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because the asset has a specific federal exemption or business use, apply the $600 joint amount to a single debtor, reject § 8123 because value exceeds its ceiling, invent a Pennsylvania-specific category, or report only a half-interest.

operations.rationale: Across current TRAIN sources the parent repeatedly omitted § 522(d)(5) after the existing reminder, often reasoning that nonresidential property could not use unused homestead capacity. The rewritten first-pass instruction makes the statutory 'any property' alternative operational for both tasks while preserving specific alternatives and their distinct amount rules.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes ILLINOIS and the debtor owns personal property that the task facts treat as personally used.
by_task.procedure: Make a separate § 12-1001(b) pass over every such asset, including necessary apparel, a motor vehicle, and a prescribed health aid, and retain § 12-1001(b) alongside every applicable specific provision. Apply § 12-1001(d) only when the facts identify use as a tool of the debtor's trade; a tool-like name alone does not establish business use when the task supplies personal use.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real property or property explicitly used for business, omit it because a specific exemption also applies, or infer trade use merely from an item's design or name.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes ILLINOIS and a debtor-owned personal-use asset requires eligibility and amount decisions.
by_task.procedure: First add § 12-1001(b) independently for every personal-use asset and report the lesser of the whole asset value and $4,000 for one debtor, or $8,000 for a jointly owned asset of two debtor spouses. Then add each supported specific alternative separately: § 12-1001(c) protects at most $2,400 of a motor vehicle without doubling that vehicle ceiling; necessary apparel under § 12-1001(a) and prescribed health aids under § 12-1001(e) use the asset's value. Use § 12-1001(d) only when trade use is stated.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not replace a specific exemption with § 12-1001(b), omit the general alternative from apparel, vehicles, or health aids, infer business use from a tool-like or work-style description, double § 12-1001(c), or leave a half-interest as the whole-asset output.

operations.rationale: The current source again omitted the general alternative from specifically described property and EV also invented trade use for a personally used toolbox. Historical sources 190, 195, and 196 show the same repeated omission, so the existing true but ineffective 'other personal property' wording requires a mandatory independent pass and an explicit factual boundary for trade use.

by_task.avoid_when: Do not require the wildcard asset itself to be a residence, suppress § 522(d)(5) because a specific exemption applies or the asset exceeds a ceiling, classify jewelry or firearms under § 522(d)(3), copy a ceiling when the asset is worth less, or double a ceiling without a joint case and a statute that applies separately.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes ILLINOIS and the debtor owns personal property that the task facts treat as personally used.
by_task.procedure: Make a separate § 12-1001(b) pass over every such asset, including necessary apparel, a motor vehicle, and a prescribed health aid, and retain § 12-1001(b) alongside every applicable specific provision. Apply § 12-1001(d) only when the facts identify use as a tool of the debtor's trade; a tool-like name alone does not establish business use when the task supplies personal use.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real property or property explicitly used for business, omit it because a specific exemption also applies, or infer trade use merely from an item's design or name.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes ILLINOIS and a debtor-owned personal-use asset requires eligibility and amount decisions.
by_task.procedure: First add § 12-1001(b) independently for every personal-use asset and report the lesser of the whole asset value and $4,000 for one debtor, or $8,000 for a jointly owned asset of two debtor spouses. Then add each supported specific alternative separately: § 12-1001(c) protects at most $2,400 of a motor vehicle without doubling that vehicle ceiling; necessary apparel under § 12-1001(a) and prescribed health aids under § 12-1001(e) use the asset's value. Use § 12-1001(d) only when trade use is stated.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not replace a specific exemption with § 12-1001(b), omit the general alternative from apparel, vehicles, or health aids, infer business use from a tool-like or work-style description, double § 12-1001(c), or leave a half-interest as the whole-asset output.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes OREGON and the debtor owns personal property.
by_task.procedure: Make a separate pass that adds Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) to every personal-property asset, including a vehicle, firearm, health aid, jewelry, apparel, and household good, while retaining all applicable category-specific Oregon and federal citations.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property, omit it because a specific exemption also applies, or use it as a substitute for the specific alternative.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes OREGON and a debtor-owned personal-property asset requires eligibility and amount decisions.
by_task.procedure: First add § 18.345(1)(p) independently and report the lesser of the whole asset value and $400. Then retain and value each supported specific alternative under its own rule, including § 18.345(1)(b) for wearing apparel or jewelry, § 18.345(1)(f) for household goods or appliances, § 18.345(1)(d) for a vehicle, § 18.345(1)(h) for a prescribed health aid, and § 18.362 for a qualifying firearm.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to a homestead or other real property, omit it because another personal-property exemption applies, treat $400 as an eligibility threshold, double its asset-level output merely because two debtors are listed, or replace the correct apparel category with the household-goods category.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes PENNSYLVANIA and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption for any property. Retain it alongside every independently applicable federal or Pennsylvania-specific exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not replace a specific exemption with § 8123, and do not cite Pennsylvania provisions for property not owned by the debtor.

by_task.when: The supplied allowable namespace includes PENNSYLVANIA and the named asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Make an independent Pennsylvania pass over every debtor-owned asset, including real property and business property, and add § 8123 whether or not another exemption applies. Report the lesser of the whole asset value and $300 for one debtor. For a jointly owned asset of two debtor spouses, § 8123 permits a combined asset-level amount up to $600, capped by value. Keep every independently eligible federal or Pennsylvania-specific alternative and calculate it under its own rule.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because the asset has a specific federal exemption or business use, apply the $600 joint amount to a single debtor, reject § 8123 because value exceeds its ceiling, invent a Pennsylvania-specific category, or report only a half-interest.
